display_name: Lafage, Côtes Catalanes Vieilles Vignes Tessellae
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "Old-vine Carignan is the spine of Tessellae, giving the wine a savory, iron-tinged core lifted by Grenache, Syrah and Monastrell. At 14.5% ABV the wine reads ripe and concentrated, the product of Roussillon sun tempered by the region's Tramontane wind.",
  "wine_summary": "Lafage works across Roussillon to blend old-vine Grenache, Carignan, Syrah and Monastrell into wines that deliver immediate fruit and regional savory notes. Tessellae matters because it packages old-vine concentration and the Côtes Catalanes' Mediterranean character into an accessible table red; the appellation allows these varieties and the bottle shows the dark fruit, dried herb and iron notes typical of old-vine Carignan. Market-wise, Tessellae sits at an everyday price point ($14.56 LCBO NV) while offering texture and density that exceed many commodity blends.",
  "terroir_expression": "Côtes Catalanes lies in Pyrénées-Orientales under a Mediterranean climate with hot, sun-soaked summers and regular Tramontane wind; vineyards in the appellation occupy a patchwork of soils—schist outcrops, clay-limestone pockets and alluvial terraces—which together yield ripe fruit, mineral lift and firm structure. That schist and clay influence explains the wine's iron and mineral edge, while the site's heat and limited water availability concentrate flavors and produce the high natural alcohol.",
  "vinification_summary": "Lafage does not publish a complete vinification sheet for Tessellae; the wine's profile—ripe dark fruit framed by firm, slightly hard-edged tannins and savory Carignan notes—points to gentle extraction and conservative use of oak plus likely blending of lots to balance power. Carbonic maceration is commonly used in modern Carignan bottlings to soften tannins (a technique where grapes ferment whole in a low-oxygen tank), and while Tessellae's exact use of that technique is not public, the softening of tannin on some vintages suggests winemaking choices intended to manage Carignan's natural bite.",
  "food_pairing": "1) Roast Catalan lamb shoulder with rosemary, garlic and anchovy — the wine's tannins and savory garrigue notes cut fat and echo the herb/olive flavors.\n2) Cassoulet (Toulouse-style with pork and duck confit) — high tannin and concentrated fruit stand up to rich, slow-cooked meats.\n3) Nashville hot chicken with pickles and white bread (casual) — ripe fruit and alcohol counter the spice while tannins tame the fried crust.\n4) Grilled chorizo-stuffed piquillo peppers with black olive tapenade (small plates) — the wine's iron-mineral grip and black fruit match the cured pork and olive saltiness.",
  "comparable_wines": "Domaine Gauby red (Roussillon) — similar use of old-vine Carignan/Grenache on schist soils producing mineral, savory reds.  Mas Janeil Vieilles Vignes (Collioure/Côtes Catalanes) — comparable old-vine Carignan/Grenache intensity and garrigue character, though often from steeper coastal sites.",
  "style_profile": "Full-bodied dry red with firm tannins and mineral-savory garrigue note",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink now through 8–12 years from vintage; younger bottles benefit from 30–60 minutes in a decanter to soften tannins. Store at 12–14°C with moderate humidity and minimal light.",
  "value_assessment": "Price: $14.56 (LCBO, NV). At this price it competes with entry-level Côtes du Rhône and other Roussillon Côtes blends (roughly $12–18). It's worth buying because you get old-vine Carignan concentration, Mediterranean garrigue and real structure that outperforms many supermarket reds in the same band.",
  "market_position": "Restaurants and retail shops that program value-driven Mediterranean reds will use this bottle on bistro lists and neighborhood wine shelves. It's aimed at casual drinkers who want bold fruit and savory, grill-friendly wines, and at buyers seeking cellarable value rather than collector provenance.",
  "insider_take": "Buy Tessellae if you want a muscular, savory Roussillon red at everyday pricing; skip it if you prefer lower-alcohol, ethereal Pinot-style reds. The tradeoff is clear: you get concentrated old-vine character and a sense of place, but the 14.5% alcohol and firm tannins can feel heavy without food or decanting.",

parsed.terroir_expression: Côtes Catalanes lies in Pyrénées-Orientales under a Mediterranean climate with hot, sun-soaked summers and regular Tramontane wind; vineyards in the appellation occupy a patchwork of soils—schist outcrops, clay-limestone pockets and alluvial terraces—which together yield ripe fruit, mineral lift and firm structure. That schist and clay influence explains the wine's iron and mineral edge, while the site's heat and limited water availability concentrate flavors and produce the high natural alcohol.
parsed.vinification_summary: Lafage does not publish a complete vinification sheet for Tessellae; the wine's profile—ripe dark fruit framed by firm, slightly hard-edged tannins and savory Carignan notes—points to gentle extraction and conservative use of oak plus likely blending of lots to balance power. Carbonic maceration is commonly used in modern Carignan bottlings to soften tannins (a technique where grapes ferment whole in a low-oxygen tank), and while Tessellae's exact use of that technique is not public, the softening of tannin on some vintages suggests winemaking choices intended to manage Carignan's natural bite.
parsed.food_pairing:
1) Roast Catalan lamb shoulder with rosemary, garlic and anchovy — the wine's tannins and savory garrigue notes cut fat and echo the herb/olive flavors.
2) Cassoulet (Toulouse-style with pork and duck confit) — high tannin and concentrated fruit stand up to rich, slow-cooked meats.
3) Nashville hot chicken with pickles and white bread (casual) — ripe fruit and alcohol counter the spice while tannins tame the fried crust.
4) Grilled chorizo-stuffed piquillo peppers with black olive tapenade (small plates) — the wine's iron-mineral grip and black fruit match the cured pork and olive saltiness.
parsed.comparable_wines: Domaine Gauby red (Roussillon) — similar use of old-vine Carignan/Grenache on schist soils producing mineral, savory reds.  Mas Janeil Vieilles Vignes (Collioure/Côtes Catalanes) — comparable old-vine Carignan/Grenache intensity and garrigue character, though often from steeper coastal sites.

parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink now through 8–12 years from vintage; younger bottles benefit from 30–60 minutes in a decanter to soften tannins. Store at 12–14°C with moderate humidity and minimal light.
parsed.value_assessment: Price: $14.56 (LCBO, NV). At this price it competes with entry-level Côtes du Rhône and other Roussillon Côtes blends (roughly $12–18). It's worth buying because you get old-vine Carignan concentration, Mediterranean garrigue and real structure that outperforms many supermarket reds in the same band.
parsed.market_position: Restaurants and retail shops that program value-driven Mediterranean reds will use this bottle on bistro lists and neighborhood wine shelves. It's aimed at casual drinkers who want bold fruit and savory, grill-friendly wines, and at buyers seeking cellarable value rather than collector provenance.
parsed.insider_take: Buy Tessellae if you want a muscular, savory Roussillon red at everyday pricing; skip it if you prefer lower-alcohol, ethereal Pinot-style reds. The tradeoff is clear: you get concentrated old-vine character and a sense of place, but the 14.5% alcohol and firm tannins can feel heavy without food or decanting.
